topic.title: Docker Containers Explained: How They Actually Work

hook: Docker containers are NOT lightweight virtual machines. They are isolated Linux processes.

slides.headline: Docker Containers Explained: What They Actually Are
slides.body: Many engineers think containers bundle an entire guest operating system. In reality, a container is just an ordinary Linux process running in an isolated namespace.
slides.visualSuggestion: Container shipping box containing process PID with isolation shields

slides.headline: Namespaces: Creating the Illusion of Isolation
slides.body: Linux namespaces partition kernel resources. PID namespaces give the container its own process tree (PID 1). NET namespaces provide a dedicated network stack, and MNT namespaces isolate the filesystem.
slides.visualSuggestion: Linux Kernel splitting PID, NET, MNT, and IPC namespaces

slides.headline: Cgroups: Enforcing Hard Resource Limits
slides.body: Control Groups (cgroups) regulate hardware utilization. They ensure a rogue container cannot exhaust host RAM, CPU cycles, or disk I/O, preventing denial of service on shared clusters.
slides.visualSuggestion: Cgroup governor capping CPU percentage and memory quota bounds

slides.headline: OverlayFS: How Layered Images Save Disk Space
slides.body: Docker images consist of read-only layers stacked via OverlayFS. When a container runs, Docker attaches a thin writable layer on top, using Copy-on-Write (CoW) to minimize storage.
slides.visualSuggestion: Read-only image layers stacked under a thin writable container layer

slides.headline: Key Takeaway: Speed, Efficiency & Portability
slides.body: Because containers share the host Linux kernel directly, they boot in milliseconds with near-zero virtualization overhead. Understand the kernel primitives to master container debugging.
slides.visualSuggestion: Process execution speed benchmark vs full hypervisor VM boot

caption: Containers are not virtual machines! Discover the core Linux primitives—namespaces, cgroups, and OverlayFS—that power Docker and modern cloud deployments.
